text: Sophronium hunc posteriorem esse priore illo altero cujus ut presbyteri meminit, descripsitque vitam sanctus Hieronymus in Scriptorum ecclesiasticorum catalogo : cum ille sancto Hieronymo σύγχρονος ad tempora Joannis 44 Hierosolymitani pontificis vixerit. Hic vero cum in sua de Christi natalitiis oratione multis agat de immani sævaque tyrannide Saracenorum qui per id tempus oppidum Bethleem occupabant, satis indicat se illum esse Sophronium 62, ac postremum Pontificem Hierosolymitanum, cujus meminit Nicephori Constantinopolitani Chronologia. Pleniora de S. Sophronio Hierosolymitano episcopo suppeditabit tomo VIII Annalium ecclesiasticorum exact. 13, sextæ synodi ex concilio Romano sub S. Martino Papa, secretario 2, tomo III. Ex Theophane in Miscella et aliis. Consule quoque notas ad Romanum Martyrologium 11 Martii. Consignatur obitus sancti Sophronii sub Heraclio imperatore, anno salutis 636, 11 Martii, quo die ejus natalis inter sanctos inscriptus habetur publicis Latinæ et Græcæ Ecclesiæ tabulis. Bibliotheca Patrum, t. XII, 206.
anchorLine: S. Sophronii (1) archiepiscopi Hierosolymitani in
en: That this Sophronius is the later one, distinct from the earlier one whom Jerome mentions as a presbyter and whose life he wrote in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers (Jerome being a contemporary of the Jerusalem bishop John), is clear: for in this oration on Christ's Nativity he speaks at length of the savage tyranny of the Saracens who at that time held Bethlehem, which shows that he is the Sophronius who was the last Patriarch of Jerusalem and who is mentioned in the Chronology of Nicephorus of Constantinople. Fuller details on St Sophronius will be given in volume VIII of the Annales ecclesiastici (year 13 [sic as printed: exact. 13]), in the acts of the sixth synod from the Roman council under St Martin the Pope (secretary 2, vol. III), from Theophanes in the Miscella, and others. See also the notes to the Roman Martyrology at 11 March. The death of St Sophronius is recorded under Emperor Heraclius, in the year of salvation 636, on 11 March, the day on which his feast is entered among the saints in the public tables of the Latin and Greek Church. Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. XII, 206.

text: Vet. Script. Nov. Collect. tom. X pag. XXV. Nil porro mirum, quod hanc homiliam inde ab anno 1666, interprete Joanne Francisco Albano, Clemente dein hujus nomine undecimo Romano pontifice, Romæ excusam fuisse, eruditissimum virum latuerit, quando id ipsum generatim scriptores historiæ litterariæ latuit : latendi autem causa haud obscura est, quod nempe opusculum ne vicenis quidem pagellis constans, atque ab adolescente septemdecim vix annos nato vulgatum, non eam de se famam potuit excitare, quæ extra Urbis mœnia longe lateque pervolitaret; unde factum est, ut cito in tenebras, e quibus emerserat, reme[…]verit, et ægre aliquod ejusdem exemplar in bibliothecarum Urbis miscellaneis reperire liceat.
anchorLine: quam necdum editam existimavit, (5),
en: Vetera Scriptorum Nova Collectio, vol. X, p. xxv. It is no wonder that this homily, published at Rome from the year 1666 in the translation of John Francis Albani (later Pope Clement XI), escaped a most learned man, since it escaped writers of literary history in general. The reason for its escape is not obscure: the little work, not even twenty pages long and published by a young man scarcely seventeen, could not raise the kind of reputation that would fly far and wide beyond the walls of the City; hence it quickly sank back into the obscurity from which it had emerged, and a copy of it is hardly to be found even in the miscellanies of the libraries of the City.

Likewise, what you read in this homily (§ 44), that God willed to keep his mother intact as he was being born, so that his divinity might thereby be proved, you will find in the Homily on Christ's Nativity (Lyons Bibliotheca Patrum, vol. anchorLine: adversasque hæreses redarguenti (16).
en: You have examples both in the opening of the Homily on the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, where, quite apart from the oration's theme, he inculcates the doctrine of Christ's two natures, and in the Sermon on the Meeting of the Lord, in which this too is worth noting: although he had already spoken at length and repeatedly (§§ 5, 8, 9, 11) against the heresies of Nestorius, Eutyches and the Acephali, he again (§ 22) takes occasion to preach the two natures of Christ from the two birds said to have been offered then (in the Bollandists, loc. cit., p. 272).

text: In Romano nostro collegio hæc propugnata est thesis : Quæ feruntur mutuæ Honorii ac Sergii epistolæ, eas aut confictas aut saltem interpolatas habendas esse affirmamus. De quo quidem argumento nonnulla aliquando me editurum confido. Illud unum hic præmoneo, momenta, quæ in hanc me sententiam impulerunt, alia esse ac hypothesim, quam de interpolatis synodi VI Actis Em. Baronius propugnavit.
anchorLine: non satis firmam esse fidem (18). Addiderim ul-
en: In our Roman College this thesis was defended: the letters said to have been exchanged between Honorius and Sergius we maintain to be either forged or at least interpolated. On this subject I trust I shall publish something in due course. I only warn here that the considerations that moved me to this view are different from the hypothesis that Cardinal Baronius advanced about the interpolated Acts of the Sixth Synod.

text: Ne, quæso, Janseniani existiment, præformatam hic a sancto Sophronio fuisse eam loquendi formulam, quæ, uti in dogmatica Constitutione Auctorem Fidei, inquit s. m. Pius VI, facile rudes præsertim et incautos in fraudem impellere valet, quippe quæ tradens, Deum in tribus personis distingui, vi verborum hoc erroris periculum subinfert, ut essentia divina distincta in personis putetur. Subjectum enim, quod in hoc Sophronii loco et distinctionem præferre dicitur, et distinctum quoad personas prædicatur, et distinctionem obtinere perhibetur, non est natura aut essentia divina, sed sacrosancta atque adoranda Trinitas. Eam autem Apostolicæ Constitutionis sententiam nunc meminisse haud inutile visum fuerit, quando formulam illam loquendi, quam SS. Pontifex graviori potius
anchorLine: distinctionem præfert (1) in hypostasibus ; et dum
en: Let the Jansenists not suppose, I beg, that Sophronius here anticipated that way of speaking which, as Pius VI of holy memory says in the dogmatic Constitution Auctorem Fidei, can easily lead the simple and unwary into error, since in teaching that God is distinguished in three persons it carries by the force of the words the danger of an error, that the divine essence is thought distinct in the persons. For the subject which in this passage of Sophronius is said to display distinction, to be called distinct as to persons, and to hold distinction, is not the divine nature or essence but the most holy and adorable Trinity. It may be of use to recall now that statement of the Apostolic Constitution, since that manner of speaking, which the Supreme Pontiff rather gravely [note continues on the next page].

text: Hæc enim, proprie et accurate loquendo, nomina sunt trium personarum, triumve hypostaseon : Ταῦτα γάρ, τῶν τριῶν προσώπων καὶ τῶν τριῶν..... ὑποστάσεων ἀκριβῶς ἐστι τὰ ὀνόματα. Ita Sophronius ; et ex hisce quoque confirmatur quam merito s. m. Pius VI, in dogmatica Constitutione Auctorem Fidei notaverit insitiam Pistoriensis conciliabuli ita de hac re statuentis, perinde ac exactior loquendi forma postularet, ut augustissimæ Triadis personæ appellarentur Pater, Verbum, Spiritus sanctus, minus vero exacte denominarentur Pater, Filius, et Spiritus sanctus. Porro si hac mere de causa, apostolicæ quidem sedis judicio, Pistoriense conciliabulum reprehensione non caruit ; quid vero sentiendum de recenti illa falsi nominis scientia, quæ (uti legimus in Petri Leroux Ἐγχυκλοπαιδεία, cap. 8,) loquendi formam æque atque ipsam dogmatis substantiam inscite juxta ac perverse corrumpens, sanctissimæ Trialis mysterium ita exhibet, ut personæ Patris locum teneat realitas entis, locum Filii entis idealitas, amor vero locum Spiritus sancti sibi vindicet ?
anchorLine: hypostaseon proprie sunt nomina (2), quibus
en: For these, speaking properly and accurately, are the names of the three persons, or of the three hypostases: "For these are precisely the names of the three persons and of the three hypostases." So Sophronius; and from this too is confirmed how rightly Pius VI of holy memory, in the dogmatic Constitution Auctorem Fidei, censured the ignorance of the Pistoian conciliabule, which ruled on this matter as though a more exact manner of speaking required that the persons of the most august Triad be called Father, Word, Holy Spirit, and less exactly Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Now if for this reason alone the Pistoian conciliabule did not escape reproof, in the judgment of the Apostolic See, what must be thought of that recent "knowledge falsely so called" which (as we read in Pierre Leroux's Encyclopedia, ch. 8), corrupting the manner of speaking and the very substance of the dogma, unskilfully and perversely, presents the mystery of the most holy Triad in such a way that the reality of being takes the place of the person of the Father, the ideality of being the place of the Son, and love the place of the Holy Spirit?
